The estate agent asked which of us had been waving from the attic during the viewing. We had spent the entire visit together in the garden.
Every morning a little more of the wallpaper pattern turns to face my bed. Tonight the flowers have teeth.
I found a photograph of tomorrow's dinner table tucked inside an old book. My place was set with a black ribbon instead of a chair.
The recording of my sleep contained eight hours of someone patiently teaching me a name. This morning I answered to it before I remembered my own.
The new neighbour keeps returning things I haven't lost yet. Today she brought my wedding ring and refused to meet my eyes.
My daughter says the woman in her dreams needs permission to come inside. This morning every mirror in the house was covered in small handprints from behind.
I watched the lift doors close on an empty car. Through the narrowing gap, something raised a finger to where its lips should have been.
The knocking followed me from wall to wall until I stepped outside. Then it started under my skin.
Someone has been replacing my childhood photographs with slightly different rooms. Today there is a door behind my cot that I remember being told never existed.
The old woman on the train asked me to stop pretending I was her son. I had not spoken to her, but I was wearing his face in the window.
Each night the shape under the sheet on the unused bed gets taller. I live alone, and I have never owned a second bed.
The doorbell camera recorded me arriving home six times yesterday. In the last recording, the thing wearing my coat finally learned how to smile.
I put flour across the nursery doorway to prove there were no footprints. By morning, something had pressed a face into it from underneath the floor.
The emergency operator told me to stay very still until the footsteps passed. Then she whispered that she could hear them on her end too.
My father died without ever hearing my new phone number. The calls began the day I stopped visiting his grave.
The shadow of the coat rack has been getting closer to the chair every evening. I moved the coat rack outside yesterday.
I woke to someone carefully measuring the length of my bed. In the morning, the same measurements were carved into the inside of the wardrobe.
The voice behind the bathroom wall always stops when I put my ear against it. Today a hand pushed back.
Everyone in the crowd was watching the fireworks except one man staring straight at my camera. He was in the previous year's photograph too, a little closer.
My reflection began crying while I brushed my teeth. When I reached towards it, it shook its head and looked behind me.
The footprints in the snow ended at our front door. They were bare, child-sized, and each one contained a tooth.
The doctor played back the heartbeat recording and asked me to identify the whispered words. I hadn't told her I could hear them.
I heard my husband come home and quietly remove his shoes. The hospital was still explaining why he wouldn't be coming home.
The stranger across the street copies every movement I make, a second too late. I closed the curtains and heard fabric slide across the inside of my window.
My son drew our family holding hands with a tall blank figure. When I asked who it was, he said it was my turn to remember.
The locked room smells increasingly of the sea. Last night, wet sand began trickling from the keyhole.
I always check the wardrobe before sleeping because of a childhood fear. Tonight something inside checked the room first.
The voice on the answering machine described where I was hiding. The message was recorded before the house was built.
At the funeral, everyone turned towards me at exactly the same moment. From inside the coffin, someone sighed with relief.
The scratches on the bedroom door were getting deeper every night. I finally realised they were being made by my own fingernails while I slept facing it.
The field behind our house has one more scarecrow every morning. Today one of them was wearing the coat I had just taken off.
The baby in the old family film looked directly into the camera and mouthed my name. I was born twenty years after the film was made.
I marked the ceiling stain with pencil to see whether it spread. By midnight the outline had moved, but the pencil marks had moved with it.
The hotel wake-up call asked whether I wanted the usual warning. Before I could answer, someone began trying every door handle along the corridor.
We found a sealed letter inside the wall addressed to whoever would find me. It described what I am wearing right now.
The cemetery caretaker asked me not to answer anyone who called from the closed section. Yesterday I heard him calling from there.
I counted the passengers reflected in the bus window and got one too many. The extra reflection noticed me counting.
My brother says he remembers the summer we buried the box in the woods. I remember burying him.
The voice outside said the password correctly, so I opened the door. I had invented the password silently, just to test it.
The tap water briefly formed a mouth against the glass. It kept trying to say something after I poured it away.
Our family photographs have started showing the backs of our heads. This morning mine was the only face still looking at the camera.
The moving company called about a child left inside one of the wardrobes. We only hired them to deliver an empty desk.
Someone has been filling my diary with apologies for things I haven't done. The last page is entirely in my mother's handwriting.
I heard the familiar rattle of my dog's collar under the kitchen table. His ashes were still warm in the box on the counter.
Every time the train passes through the tunnel, one passenger forgets who they are. The conductor has started carrying extra name tags.
I recognised my own handwriting on a missing-person poster. The photograph showed me standing behind whoever was reading it.
The woman in the flat opposite has been standing at her window for three days. When the lights went out, her face stayed illuminated from inside.
The lighthouse beam passed across my bedroom wall and revealed a row of people facing the corner. We live hundreds of miles inland.
I woke to the feeling of someone sitting at the foot of my bed. The mattress rose slowly as the weight moved up onto the ceiling.
The piano played the same unfinished tune every night after we inherited it. Last night something beneath the floor sang the ending.
My hands stopped moving in the mirror while I washed them. The reflection carefully dried its hands and walked out of view.
The child on the playground asked why I kept leaving him here. His school uniform was the one I had worn when I disappeared for a week.
The noise in the chimney was too regular to be an animal. When I held my breath, it began breathing for me.
The tour guide asked us to count the statues before leaving the crypt. I counted one less each time I looked away.
The shadow beneath the bathroom door was wearing my slippers. I was still wearing them too.
The last page of the house inspection report was a detailed drawing of a room behind my bedroom. In the drawing, I was already asleep inside it.
I found a child's height marks on the inside of the cellar door. The highest one was dated tomorrow and was taller than the door.
Our new clock doesn't tick when anyone is watching it. When I closed my eyes, I heard it running across the shelf.
The recorded announcement asked passengers not to acknowledge the woman between stations. Every face in the carriage slowly turned towards me.
The hospital visitor register contained my name for every day of the past year. The signatures matched, but I had never been inside before today.
The dark patch at the bottom of the swimming pool moved against the water. The lifeguard quietly asked everyone to stop casting shadows.
A man has appeared at the edge of every dream I've had this month. Last night he handed me a key that was still in my fist when I woke.
My wife keeps asking why I stare at the empty chair. I haven't told her the person in it asks the same question about her.
The scratch on my glasses looks exactly like a tiny open door. Through it, the room contains someone standing immediately behind my chair.
The little girl in the lift asked which floor the people who replaced us live on. Every button was already pressed except ours.
I watched my sleeping husband's chest rise once, then twice at different speeds. Something underneath was trying to match his breathing.
The voice from the well said it was cold and needed my coat. When I refused, it described the clothes I would be buried in.
My dentist asked who had sewn the small black thread behind my last tooth. I felt it tighten when I tried to answer.
We started hearing music from the flat below after the building was evacuated. The tune stops whenever one of us remembers the lyrics.
I took the batteries out of the talking doll before packing it away. In the dark, a much older voice thanked me for the quiet.
My missing sister came home knowing every family secret except her own name. We still set a place for her, because she watches to make sure.
The thing following us never appeared in the torchlight. We only saw it when the shadows of all three of us turned to look back.
I leaned against the sealed doorway and heard a party on the other side. Someone raised a toast to the last day they would have to pretend to be me.
The empty cot rocked whenever my mother told her childhood stories. Tonight it rocked before she opened her mouth.
There was an extra step on the staircase this morning. Everyone else insists it has always been there, but they won't step on it.
The man at the photograph counter refused to develop my film. He said the person holding the camera appeared in every picture.
The postman asked me to stop answering the door in different voices. I work nights and sleep through the deliveries.
Someone keeps cleaning a small circle in the dust under my bed. Tonight it was large enough for a face.
The nursery rhyme from next door stopped halfway through a line. The rest of it was whispered from inside my mouth.
I found a receipt for the exact time I woke last night. The item description was SECOND ATTEMPT.
The blindfolded statue in the town square is facing our house now. This morning its hands were resting on the knot.
The rain on the window began running upwards one drop at a time. Behind each drop, a tiny eye stayed level with mine.
My father taught me a knock that meant it was safe to open the cellar. He never taught me what to do when the cellar knocked first.
The voice at the door said it had found my body. I heard my own voice behind it begging me not to ask where.
I found a jar labelled with my name in the abandoned classroom. Every time I loosened the lid, I forgot another year.
The dream always ended when the faceless nurse reached my bed. Last night she stopped at the doorway and said she would finish during visiting hours.
I woke with a long white hair tied around each wrist. The locked bedroom window was open just wide enough for fingers.
My grandmother's recordings contain a pause wherever she says my name. In the pauses, someone else is learning to pronounce it.
The marks inside the cupboard looked like tally lines until I recognised the dates. Every one was a night I had slept well.
The new tenant asked whether we could stop walking above his ceiling at night. His flat is directly above ours.
I saw my mother standing very still at the far end of the supermarket aisle. When she turned, all the other shoppers turned with her.
The house across the field always has its lights on when I close my eyes. Last night I could see someone crossing the field between blinks.
The missing child was returned with exactly the same clothes and memories. Only the family dog remembers why we shouldn't let him upstairs.
I heard someone practising my laugh through the heating vent. They stopped needing to practise three days ago.
A warm hand covered my eyes while I was washing my face. In the mirror I could see my own hands still pressed against my cheeks.
The car park attendant handed me a ticket already stamped EXITED. Behind him, every parked car had someone sitting motionless in the driver's seat.
The last house on the street has been demolished for years. Today its curtains were visible in every window on our side of the road.
The old tape contained a recording of my first words. After the adults stopped cheering, a voice very close to the microphone said they would do.
I pressed my ear to the bedroom door and heard someone doing the same. Then the door became warm and began to pulse.
The empty chair at our table has been pulled out a little further each evening. Tonight my family asked me to stop sitting in it.
